issues.body: validate_policy_for_n3 still checks only that prohibition action/target/assignee are present; it does not enforce exactly-one cardinality for those fields on permissions or prohibitions. The new unambiguous_operands guard covers constraint-node operands/combinators, not rule attributes. Rust parsing selects one action/target/assignee, whereas odrl-d.n3 and the prohibition strata can match any asserted value. A policy with two assignees, actions, or targets can therefore produce an N3 grant that the Rust reference path does not, contradicting the documented never-more-permissive property. The generated differential cannot catch this because generate_policy always emits exactly one value for every rule attribute.
issues.fix_hint: For every permission and prohibition rule, reject unless odrl:action, odrl:target, and odrl:assignee each have exactly one distinct object, or implement identical multi-value semantics in both paths. Add a public-path differential regression with two assignees and preferably action/target variants that demonstrates the Rust-selected value and asserts the N3 call refuses with the graph unchanged (or returns exactly the same no-grant result). Extend the generated corpus with multi-valued rule-attribute shapes.
issues.title: Multi-valued rule attributes still allow N3 authorization widening

verdict.summary: Round 5 is stagnant. The round-4 authorization-widening finding remains: validation still does not require exactly one odrl:action, odrl:target, and odrl:assignee on each permission/prohibition rule. The N3 rules existentially match every value, while the Rust policy parser/evaluator collapses these fields to one value, so a second matching value can let N3 grant where Rust does not. The new ambiguity guard applies only to constraint operands/combinators, and the generated corpus always emits one action, target, and assignee, so it does not exercise this discrepancy.
